title: YOU ASKED GOD FOR MORE YEARS—BUT WHAT ARE YOU DOING WITH THE BODY HE GAVE YOU?
paragraphs: YOU ASKED GOD FOR MORE YEARS—BUT WHAT ARE YOU DOING WITH THE BODY HE GAVE YOU?

You pray for health. You ask God to protect your life. You want to see your children grow, hold your grandchildren, finish your calling, and live long enough to become everything Christ is shaping you to become. But what happens when your prayers are asking for life while your habits keep walking toward destruction?
There is a prayer almost nobody hears.
It happens quietly.
Sometimes before sleep.
Sometimes after a frightening medical result.
Sometimes after the chest tightens, the coughing gets worse, the body feels different, or someone we love dies far too young.
“Lord, please give me more time.”
“Lord, keep me healthy.”
“Lord, let me live long enough to see my children grow.”
“Jesus, please heal me.”
And sometimes, after saying amen, the same hand that was lifted toward heaven reaches again for the cigarette.
The bottle opens again.
The substance returns.
The destructive habit gets another night.
And tomorrow, the prayer begins again.
This is not written to humiliate you.
It is written because sometimes love has to ask the question nobody wants to ask:
What if you are asking God to protect the life you are refusing to steward?
That question hurts.
But perhaps it needs to.
Because grace does not merely comfort us while we destroy ourselves.
Grace teaches us to live differently.
Paul wrote:
“For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions…” — Titus 2:11–12
Grace saves.
Grace forgives.
But grace also trains.
It confronts.
It changes direction.
It teaches the person who has been rescued not to keep walking willingly toward the chains Christ is calling them out of.
Maybe your struggle is smoking.
Maybe alcohol has quietly become something more than an occasional drink.
Maybe it is drugs.
Maybe it is another vice nobody knows about.
Maybe everybody around you thinks you are fine.
You still work.
You still laugh.
You still post Bible verses.
You may still attend church.
You may even serve.
But there is something you keep returning to when the loneliness gets heavy.
Something you reach for when anxiety screams.
Something that gives you ten minutes of relief and then asks you to pay for those ten minutes with another piece of yourself.
And somewhere beneath all the excuses, you already know.
This is not freedom.
Jesus said:
“Everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin.” — John 8:34
The Greek wording is piercing:
πᾶς ὁ ποιῶν τὴν ἁμαρτίαν δοῦλός ἐστιν τῆς ἁμαρτίας
pas ho poiōn tēn hamartian doulos estin tēs hamartias
The word δοῦλος — doulos carries the sense of a slave, someone under another's mastery.
That is what destructive habits eventually want.
Not merely participation.
Mastery.
They whisper, “You can stop whenever you want.”
Then one day you discover that wanting to stop and actually stopping are two very different things.
The cigarette starts as something you hold.
Eventually, it can feel like something that holds you.
The bottle begins as something you control.
Eventually, you may begin organizing your emotions, evenings, relationships, money, and decisions around it.
The vice says, “I will help you cope.”
Then it becomes another thing you need help coping with.
And Jesus does not expose slavery because He enjoys condemning slaves.
He exposes slavery because He came to set captives free.
A few verses later He says:
“So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.” — John 8:36
That is the heartbeat of this message.
Not shame.
Freedom.
Not “Look how terrible you are.”
But:
Look how precious you are to Christ—and ask yourself why you keep surrendering yourself to something that is destroying you.
Scripture gives Christians a powerful theology of the body.
Paul writes:
In Greek, Paul says:
δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν
doxasate dē ton Theon en tō sōmati hymōn
“Glorify God in your body.”
Read that slowly.
In your body.
Christianity is not merely about what happens inside your thoughts.
God cares about what we do with our bodies.
But we also need to handle this passage honestly.
In its immediate context, Paul is confronting sexual immorality, so we should not pretend that 1 Corinthians 6 was originally written specifically about cigarettes, alcohol, or modern addictions.
It wasn't.
Yet the theological principle Paul gives remains profound: the Christian's body belongs to Christ. We were “bought with a price,” and therefore our embodied lives should honor God.
That changes the question.
Instead of only asking,
“Is this technically allowed?”
we begin asking,
“Does this honor the Christ who purchased me?”
Instead of,
“How much can I get away with?”
we ask,
“Is this mastering me?”
Paul gives us language for that too:
“‘All things are lawful for me,’ but I will not be dominated by anything.” — 1 Corinthians 6:12
“I will not be dominated.”
That sentence belongs in the heart of anyone fighting addiction.
Because some things do not announce themselves as masters.
They arrive disguised as relief.
A drink after a difficult day.
A cigarette when stress becomes unbearable.
A substance when memories refuse to stay buried.
One more night.
One more escape.
One more promise that tomorrow will be different.
Then tomorrow becomes next week.
Next week becomes next year.
And eventually you realize you have spent years praying for God to extend a life while repeatedly feeding something capable of shortening or damaging it.

Smoking is not harmless. Tobacco use is a major preventable cause of disease and premature death. Excessive alcohol use also carries serious health risks, and other addictive substances can devastate physical health, judgment, relationships, finances, and spiritual life.
But this article is not saying that every illness is caused by personal sin.
It is not.
Faithful Christians get cancer.
People who care for their bodies still become sick.
Children become ill.
Genetics matter.
Environment matters.
Disease exists in a fallen world.
And Scripture never gives us permission to look at every suffering person and declare, “You caused this.”
Jesus Himself rejected simplistic assumptions connecting particular suffering with particular personal sin.
So this is not condemnation of sick people.
This is a confrontation with something different:
knowingly continuing destructive behavior while repeatedly asking God to protect us from its consequences.
Imagine someone standing in heavy rain praying,
“God, please keep me dry,”
while refusing the shelter directly beside him.
Sometimes God's answer to our prayer is not mysterious.
Sometimes part of the answer is repentance.
Sometimes it is throwing away the cigarettes.
Sometimes it is admitting that “social drinking” stopped being social a long time ago.
Sometimes it is telling another human being the secret.
Sometimes it is entering treatment.
Sometimes it is seeing a doctor.
Sometimes it is joining a recovery community.
Sometimes it is finally saying:
“I cannot defeat this alone.”
And that sentence is not defeat.
Sometimes that is where freedom begins.
Because repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
The New Testament often uses the word μετάνοια — metanoia for repentance, carrying the idea of a changed mind that results in a changed direction.
Biblical repentance does not say only:
“I feel bad.”
It says:
“By God's grace, I cannot keep walking this direction.”
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Condemnation says, “Hide from God.”
Conviction says, “Come home.”
Condemnation says, “You are filthy, so stay away.”
The Gospel says Christ came precisely for sinners who could never clean themselves enough to deserve Him.
“For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly.” — Romans 5:6
Not when we were impressive.
Not when every addiction had disappeared.
Not when every habit had been conquered.
While we were weak.
Jesus Christ did not climb onto a cross because humanity had successfully repaired itself.
He went there because we couldn't.
He bore sin.
He suffered.
He died.
And He rose again.
The Gospel is not behavior modification dressed in religious vocabulary.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Forgiven.
Redeemed.
Made new.
And because salvation is grace, transformation does not become optional decoration.
The Christ who forgives us also calls us to follow Him.
Maybe you have tried quitting before.
Seven times.
Twenty times.
Maybe you threw everything away on Monday and bought it again Thursday.
Maybe you prayed at an altar.
Maybe you cried.
Maybe you promised your spouse.
Maybe your child once looked at you and said, “Please stop.”
And you meant it when you promised.
Then the craving came.
The stress came.
The loneliness came.
The withdrawal came.
And you fell again.
Listen carefully:
A relapse does not mean you should stop running toward Christ.
Run toward Him again.
But do not turn grace into permission to remain passive.
Seek help.
Bring the darkness into light.

Talk with a qualified medical professional, especially when dependence is involved. Abruptly stopping heavy or prolonged alcohol use can be medically dangerous for some people, so getting professional guidance can be important.
Tell a trusted mature believer.
Ask people to pray with you.
Remove access where possible.
Learn your triggers.
Change routines.
Accept accountability.
Get appropriate treatment when needed.
Pray fiercely—and then cooperate with the opportunities for change God places before you.
There is no spiritual virtue in refusing legitimate help.
Luke, the writer of a Gospel and Acts, is identified by Paul as “the beloved physician” in Colossians 4:14.
Prayer and responsible care of the body are not enemies.
You can pray while seeing the doctor.
You can trust Christ while entering recovery.
You can believe in God's power while asking another believer to hold you accountable.
You can cry out for deliverance while taking practical steps away from what enslaves you.
And if your battle is alcohol, biblical accuracy matters here too.

Scripture does not teach that every consumption of alcohol is inherently sinful. Jesus' first sign in John's Gospel involved wine, and Paul instructed Timothy concerning a little wine for his stomach.
But Scripture unmistakably condemns drunkenness.
“And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit.” — Ephesians 5:18
The contrast is stunning.
Do not be controlled by intoxication.
Be filled with the Spirit.
So the question cannot merely be:
“Can a Christian drink?”
For some people, the far more urgent question is:
“What is this doing to me?”
Is it mastering you?
Are you hiding how much you consume?
Are relationships suffering?
Are you using it to numb pain rather than confronting that pain?
Are you repeatedly drunk?
Are you becoming someone your sober self would grieve?
Are you calling something “freedom” that has become bondage?
Then perhaps you already know what needs to happen.
There may be a bottle somewhere near you.
A pack in your pocket.
Something hidden in a drawer.
Something stored where your family will not find it.
And perhaps this article reached you while you were asking God for another chance.
Here is the scandal of grace:
You may have wasted years, but Jesus is still calling your name.
Peter denied Him.
The thief beside Him had no lifetime left to repair.
Paul had persecuted His people.
Yet grace reached into scandal and wrote redemption where human beings expected only condemnation.
That does not make sin small.
It makes the Savior enormous.
This is why our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior remains:
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because repentance guarantees a certain number of years.
Not because Christians who live carefully will never become sick.
God has never promised us immunity from mortality.
Our hope is greater than longevity.
Our hope is Christ.
Jesus said:
“I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live.” — John 11:25
Christian hope is ultimately not “God, keep me alive forever here.”
It is:
“Jesus, whether I live or die, I belong to You.”
And precisely because our lives belong to Him, the days we have should matter.
Your body is not eternal in its present condition.
But it matters.
Your lungs matter.
Your mind matters.
Your family matters.
Your witness matters.
Your remaining years matter.
And perhaps the question tonight is not whether God can forgive everything behind you.
In Christ, forgiveness is astonishingly deep.
Perhaps the question is whether you will finally stop using tomorrow as an excuse.
Tomorrow.
Tomorrow.
Tomorrow.
How many promises have died inside that word?
What if repentance begins today?
Not with a dramatic social-media declaration.
Not with pretending you will never struggle again.
But with one truthful prayer:

“Jesus, I have been asking You for life while holding tightly to something that is hurting me. Forgive me. I cannot free myself by willpower alone. Give me courage to repent, wisdom to seek help, and strength to take the next faithful step.”
Maybe your next faithful step is disposing of the cigarettes.
Maybe it is calling your doctor.
Maybe it is admitting your drinking to your spouse.
Maybe it is asking your pastor for help.
Maybe it is entering treatment.
Maybe it is texting someone tonight:
“Please don't judge me. I need help.”
Do it.
You do not need another year of hiding.
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
And when you see someone else write those words, do not mock them.
Pray.
Encourage them.
Remind them that Christ is greater than the chains around them.

Supporting Gospel work can be one meaningful way to steward what God has entrusted to you, but never confuse supporting a ministry with purchasing God's favor. Grace cannot be bought. Salvation cannot be purchased.
If you want to support the mission and go deeper:
Give yourself to Christ.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Follow Jesus.
Because eventually every cigarette burns out.
Every bottle empties.
Every temporary high comes down.
Every human body reaches its final day.
But Jesus Christ remains.
So when you kneel tonight and ask God for health…
when you ask Him for another twenty years…
when you ask Him to let you watch your children grow…
remember that prayer may require something from you—not payment for God's mercy, but a response to it.
Open your hands.
Release what has been mastering you.
Ask for help.
Walk toward freedom.
And when you fall, run back to Christ rather than back to the thing that promised relief and gave you chains.
Follow because none of us outgrows our need for Scripture.
One article cannot transform a heart.
But Jesus Christ can.
Perhaps you have spent years asking God to add days to your life.
Maybe tonight, God is confronting you with a different question:
“Will you give the days you already have back to Me?”
Because the habit may know your weakness…
but Jesus still knows your name.
